youtube.title: Equivalent Fractions for Kids | Same Amount, New Name | Grade 4 Math | Toy Box Friends
youtube.description:
Mouse ordered one half and Squirrel ordered four eighths. Who got more cake? Robo, Owl and the Slicer find out: cut every piece into equal smaller pieces and the cake never changes, only its name.
Kids learn why 1/2 = 2/4 = 4/8, the times rule (multiply the top and bottom by the same number), why adding 1 to both does not work, the fraction wall, equivalent fractions on a number line, and how to compare 3/4 and 5/8 by renaming.
Try at home: fold paper strips into halves, fourths and eighths, colour 1, 2 and 4 parts and line them up. No scissors needed; if you cut strips, ask a grown-up to help.

do.text: Equivalent Fractions Bakery
Welcome to Robo's Bakery! Two orders are ready.
Half a cake bar, please!
And four eighths for me!
Four pieces! I got more than you!
No way. My one piece is bigger!
Hmm. Let's look at the evidence.
Who really got more cake? Let's find out.
Every fraction starts with a whole. Here is one whole cake bar.
Cut it into two equal parts. Shade one part.
The bottom number counts the equal parts in the whole.
The top number counts the shaded parts. One half.
Here are two halves. Are they the same amount?
Same amount?
No! The top bar is a smaller whole, so its half is smaller.
So from now on, every bar is the same whole. Same size, every time.
same whole
Fun fact: fraction comes from a Latin word that means to break.
Meet the Slicer! It cuts every piece into equal smaller pieces. No blades, just magic.
Here is one half. Two equal parts, one shaded.
This gold line shows how much cake is shaded. Watch if it changes.
I'll slice every piece into 2. How many pieces will there be?
Four equal pieces, and two are shaded. Two fourths!
And the gold line? Exactly the same length. Same cake!
Slice every piece in 2 again!
Eight pieces, four shaded. Four eighths!
One half, two fourths, four eighths. More pieces, smaller pieces, same amount.
Now one third. Three equal parts, one shaded. Slice each piece in 2.
Six parts, two shaded. One third is the same as two sixths.
Let's start again with one third. This time, slice every piece into 3!
Nine parts, three shaded. Three ninths. Still one third of the same cake.
So, Mouse and Squirrel. Let's put your cake side by side.
Oh! My four eighths are just as long as your half.
Same amount! We both got half the cake bar.

scenes.title: Why it works: the times rule

do.text: Why does slicing keep the amount the same? Let's look closely.
Slicing every piece in 2 makes twice as many pieces in the whole.
So the bottom number doubles. Two times two is four.
The shaded pieces double too. So the top number doubles. One times two is two.
But each piece is half as big. So the amount stays the same.
The times rule: multiply the top and the bottom by the same number.
multiply top and bottom by the same number
Music has fractions too. One half note lasts as long as two quarter notes.
Three fourths: times 2 on top and bottom makes six eighths.
Two thirds: slice every piece into 4. Times 4 makes eight twelfths.
Two fifths, times 2, is four tenths. Same cake every time.
We can go backwards too. Eight twelfths: join the pieces in groups of 4.
Divide the top and bottom by 4. Two thirds! That's the simplest form.
simplest form
I have a faster way! Just add 1 to the top and the bottom.
One half, add one to both, makes two thirds. Easy!
Let's test it. Same whole, side by side.
Same amount?
Two thirds is longer. That's more cake, not the same amount.
Maybe it works for three fourths? Add one to both: four fifths.
Four fifths is longer again. Adding changes the amount.
Multiplying keeps it. One half times two is two fourths. Exactly the same length.
Got it. Never add. Multiply the top and bottom by the same number.
multiply, don't add

scenes.title: The fraction wall and the number line

do.text: Here's a fraction wall. Every row is the same whole, cut into equal parts.
Halves, thirds, fourths, sixths and eighths. Let's shade one half in every way we can.
Now a straight line down from the end of one half.
It touches two fourths, three sixths and four eighths. They are all equivalent.
But no number of thirds lands on that line.
Fun fact: ancient Egyptians wrote most fractions with a 1 on top, like one third.
Fractions are numbers on a number line too. Mouse, leap to one half.
I'll leap by eighths. One, two, three, four eighths!
Look! Same spot. One half and four eighths are the same number.
Thirds on top, sixths below. Two thirds and four sixths?
Same spot again. Equivalent fractions name the same point on the line.
Clap along! Slice it again, the cake's the same.
Times the top and bottom, a brand new name!
More pieces?
More pieces?
Smaller pieces!
Same cake?
Same cake?
Same amount!
Slice it again, the cake's the same. Times the top and bottom, a brand new name!
Order up! Each order needs a new name. Guess the missing number, then the Slicer checks.
Three fourths, please, in eighths!
Slice every piece in 2. Three becomes six.
Two fifths, in tenths, please!
Fifths to tenths: times 2. Two becomes four.
One third, in sixths, please!
Thirds to sixths: times 2. One becomes two.
Six twelfths, but in the simplest name!
Divide the top and bottom by 6. Six becomes one, twelve becomes two.
Four orders, four perfect names. Great baking, team!
Challenge! Which is more, three fourths or five eighths?
Rename three fourths in eighths. Times 2 makes six eighths.
Six eighths is more than five eighths. So three fourths is more!
Quick one! Two thirds or five sixths?
Two thirds is four sixths, and five sixths is more.
Quiz time! One: is two fourths more than, less than, or equal to one half?
Equal! Same amount, different name.
Two: three fifths equals how many tenths?
Six tenths. Times 2 on the top and the bottom.
Three: I say one third equals two fourths, because I added 1 to both. True?
False! Multiply, don't add. One third equals two sixths.
Four: which is more, three fourths or five eighths?
Three fourths, because it equals six eighths.
Remember: same whole, equal parts.
